newsitem.title: UK: INTERVIEW - Hambros confident in its strategy.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Hambros confident in its strategy.

text.p: British investment banking group Hambros Plc said on Wednesday it was confident it had taken the right steps to ensure a healthy future for the firm.
"We have great confidence in ourselves and what we are trying to do," Sir Chips Keswick, the group's chief executive, told Reuters in an interview.

In response to a question about the possibility of Hambros being a takeover target for a larger international player, Keswick said being a public company always involved being in the firing line, but he was happy with the group's direction.

Earlier Hambros reported pretax profits for the first half of 35.0 million stg, a swing from a 7.7 million stg loss for the same period in 1995. It said it would pay a maintained interim dividend of 2.5 pence per share.
Some analysts had forecast pretax profits for the period of 45.0 million stg and an interim dividend range of between 2.5 and 3.0 pence.
Keswick said that while he could not talk for the group's shareholders, he had the impression from discussions with them that they were supportive of changes implemented by Hambros.
Keswick dismissed an attempt by Hong Kong investment manager Regent Pacific Group, which holds three percent of the firm, to break up Hambros in an attempt to realise shareholder value.
"Regent is a three percent shareholder and is perfectly entitled to (its) views. We are perfectly entitled not to share them," Keswick said.

He said the group was on track to replace "low margin vanilla business" with "increased return per customer" business, adding that it had decided the best strategy was to undergo major upheavals for a year rather than piecemeal changes over a longer period in order to achieve this.

Keswick, who said the benefits of the changes could take a year or two to come through, said he was pleased the group had moved to a profit from a loss, adding that the Investment Group's result had been particularly good.
But the group's chairman, Lord Hambro, warned that profits from this part of the business were not expected to match the first half in the second.
